The United States is one of only a few countries in the world that does not guarantee paid maternity leave to its citizens. This policy has been a subject of debate for years, with many arguing that it is unfair to expect new mothers to take unpaid time off from work. In this essay, I will provide a casual summary of the U.S. maternity leave policy, with two sections (Section 1 and Section 2) and at least 25 sentences.
Section 1: The Basics of U.S. Maternity Leave Policy
The Family and Medical Leave Act (FMLA) was passed in 1993 and provides eligible employees with up to 12 weeks of unpaid leave for the birth or adoption of a child. The FMLA also covers leave for the care of a seriously ill family member or for the employee's own serious health condition. However, the FMLA does not guarantee paid leave, and many employers do not offer paid maternity leave to their employees. As a result, many new mothers are forced to choose between taking unpaid leave or returning to work immediately after giving birth.
The FMLA also has some limitations. For example, it only applies to employers with 50 or more employees, and it does not cover self-employed individuals or those who work for small businesses. Additionally, the leave is unpaid, which means that new mothers may have to rely on savings or other sources of income to support themselves and their families during this time.

They argue that Muhammad had designated Ali as his successor on several occasions, including during the Farewell Sermon at the end of his life. The Shi'a believe that the leadership of the Muslim community should be hereditary, passing from Muhammad to Ali and then to his descendants.
## Theological Differences
